doc.title: Art Farmer — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Sun Ra and Eric Dolphy
summary: Dolphy as a close friend from Los Angeles who found his voice with Mingus.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: This is 1959, 1960 and right around the corner, John Coltrane, Eric Dolphy. Had you seen Sun Ra because he was also pioneering new expressions?
No, he wasn’t around at that time. He was still out in Chicago. Sun Ra came around here like in the late 50s, and he brought some guys with him from Chicago.
What did you think of John Coltrane and Eric Dolphy when they played music that…
Eric Dolphy and I were very close friends out in California.
Yeah, with Roy Porter’s band. We were trying to unravel the shit and figure out what we could do [laughs].
Was there any indication of Eric’s direction that early on?

No, not really. The only thing that I saw about Eric was that Eric was like Trane. He was like 99% music. Only indication was that to him any song could have some musical value almost. Like birds singing in the park, he would listen to that and that’s

what he would play that night on his gig. But then, he really found himself working with Mingus because until he worked with Mingus, he was just playing within the conventional framework, such as what I was doing and everybody else from our time. He applied himself, very concentrated to music and to the horns. Working with Mingus gave him the freedom to go whichever way he wanted to go. After Mingus, he hooked up with Trane, and they were two kindred souls really.
